articles.title: ‘Call My Agent! The Movie’ Review: Love-Hate Energy Keeps the Gang Together in a Fast, Funny Feature-Length Return
articles.summary: The rare reboot pitch that that can actually be greeted with “this again!” rather than “this again?,” “Call My Agent! The Movie” makes sense of its rote title in two ways.
body: Six years after the French Netflix smash closed the doors on the ASK talent agency, we return to follow ex-agent Andréa (Camille Cottin) through the wringer of her directorial debut.

Doing very well for themselves indeed are former ASK hotshot Mathias (Thibault de Montalembert), still representing A-list talent at the new agency he founded with his daughter Camille (Fanny Sidney), and his erstwhile assistant turned wife Noémie ( Laure Calamy ), who has found surprising success as a TV producer. His old office rival Andréa, meanwhile, is happy to have left agenting behind for a more creative career as a writer-director, though as her debut feature “The Fugitive” (not a remake of the Harrison Ford vehicle) enters pre-production, she despairs to find herself putting out fires all too familiar from her former line of work.

articles.title: Big tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?
articles.summary: Its moguls are ripe subjects for drama, and there is huge anticipation for forthcoming features The Social Reckoning and Artificial. But other projects have failed as the film industry is increasingly colonised by IT empires.
body: ‘I know there are easier enemies to make,” tech reporter Jeremy Allen White tells his colleague in a recent trailer for The Social Reckoning. “The mafia would be an easier enemy to make,” comes the reply. They’re talking about Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta, but they might as well be discussing big tech as a whole. As The Social Reckoning promises to underline, it’s become clear that these people are not on our side – “us” being the whole of humanity except billionaire tech overlords and their mates. But for an industry that loves a clear-cut baddie, Hollywood has barely landed a blow on the tech industry. Now it finds itself in mortal danger of being absorbed by it. Is it too late to fight back?
points: Its moguls are ripe subjects for drama, and there is huge anticipation for forthcoming features The Social Reckoning and Artificial.

articles.summary: Laura Dern is set to give the Laudatio speech honoring George Clooney at Venice Film Festival where, as previously announced, he will be honored on Wed., Sept. 2, with a Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement.
body: Dern in 2025 was part of the cast of Noah Baumbach’s “Jay Kelly,” alongside Clooney that competed in Venice. She previously attended the Venice Film Festival multiple times with “Haunted Summer” (1988) by Ivan Passer; “October Sky” (1998) by Joe Johnston; “Dr. T & the Women” (2000) by Robert Altman; “Inland Empire” (2006) and “Marriage Story” (2019) by Noah Baumbach, for which she went on to win the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. More recently, Dern was in Venice with “The Son” (2022) by Florian Zeller. In 2006 Dern presented the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement to David Lynch.

articles.title: ’17’ Review: Harrowing Teen Pregnancy Drama from Macedonia Could Be the Feel-Bad Movie of the Year
articles.summary: From the first frame, Kosara Mitić’s “17” refuses to pull any punches, plunging us immediately into the traumatic moment when a hookup between high-school student Sara (Eva Kostić) and two boys takes a violent turn.
body: Sarajevo Best Actress winner Eva Kostić captivates in this unflinching portrait of peer pressure and sexual shame by first time writer-director Kosara Mitić.

When the group arrives by bus, Sara is a conspicuously surly presence in her baggy sweatshirt and dragging jeans; her classmates, brusque, yappy, and shockingly entitled as they constantly talk back to their two teacher-chaperones, both grossly resigned to their students’ insolence. Denied the private room she paid double for because of a mix-up by hotel management, Sara must room with her guileless, overly eager friend Lina (Martina Danilovska) and her cool-girl ex bestie Nina (Eva Stojcevska). Nina is now dating the apish Filip (Dame Joveski), Sara’s ex and one of her rapists — unbeknownst to everyone, of course.

articles.title: 10 Best '70s Movies That Could Never Be Made Today
articles.summary: Plenty of films in the 1970s challenged audiences with provocative material, and even though these movies are revered now, they'd never be made today.
body: Here are 10 movies from the 1970s that couldn't be made today.

"Deliverance" features the kind of pensive, shocking, and dark subject matter that major studios don't pursue as heavily today, and its production was dangerous as all get out. The story of four civilized men from the city who seek to canoe down the rapids of a soon-to-be-dammed river and come face-to-face with the random violence and savagery of the natural world was shot on location in Rabun County, Georgia, and you can feel the real-life peril of the actors performing dangerous in-camera stunts.

Warner Bros. was already nervous about the John Boorman-directed film's thematic content during production, and they slashed the budget. That led the main performers to do it themselves: Jon Voight got shots of him actually free-climbing the cliffside, Burt Reynolds wanted a go at being in one of the canoes as it went over a waterfall, and Ned Beatty nearly drowned while shooting other footage of the rapids. A huge fistfight also broke out on set, though that was more of an occupational hazard related to stubborn creatives than dying at the hands of nature.
points: Plenty of films in the 1970s challenged audiences with provocative material, and even though these movies are revered now, they'd never be made today.

articles.title: Gilligan's Island Star Tina Louise Starred In An Important '60s Movie Worth Revisiting
articles.summary: Right after Gilligan's Island came to an end Tina Louise starred with Sharon Tate in a very important movie from the 1960s worth revisiting.
body: Phil Karlson's 1968 film "The Wrecking Crew" was the fourth and final Matt Helm movie. It was preceded by "The Silencers" (1966), "Murderers' Row" (also 1966), and "The Ambushers" (1967). The original Matt Helm spy novels by author Donald Hamilton were notoriously gritty and violent, and the Matt Helm character was a stern, jaded, uncaring spy who always got the job done. In the movies, Matt Helm was played by Dean Martin, and the stories were adapted into goofy, campy, sexy comedy romps. Although very different from the source material, the Matt Helm movies are a blast to watch, and it's hard not to giggle at Martin's antics and be dazzled by his unbearably attractive co-stars.

articles.title: Not Everyone Likes The Federation: Star Trek's Maquis Explained
articles.summary: The Federation is typically seen as a positive organization in the Star Trek universe, but it's not perfect. The Maquis are a consequence of that imperfection.
body: Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

But, as seen in the two-part "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine" episode "The Maquis," there are those in the Federation who resent the organization, as it often fails at its job. Because the Federation isn't devoted to combat, they aren't necessarily well-equipped to rattle their sabers when dealing with a violent, devious, warlike species who would be all too happy to start fighting. Say, the Cardassians. And if the Federation's skilled negotiators have to "peacefully" cede some of their own worlds to the Cardassians as part of a potential peace deal, well, the citizens of those worlds just might be a little miffed to be suddenly living under Cardassian rule.

Those citizens might even form their own anti-Cardassian terrorist fighting force, even if the Federation doesn't approve. The force, called the Maquis, would be hated by both the Federation and the Cardassians.
The Maquis serve as a major part of "Deep Space Nine" and, later, "Star Trek: Voyager."
points: The Federation is typically seen as a positive organization in the Star Trek universe, but it's not perfect.
